corpus.title: bp task stamp read-back says the store holds a criterion the published row does not hold — evidence containing %{ lost twice

content.description:
TRAP HIT BY lead-reconcile-2 (2026-09-02), reproduced twice on task-bb83570ba0f6f9f2 against guerrilla with the installed bp (local-cf3151b0).

`bp task stamp <id> <worker> <epoch> --criterion 0 --met --criterion-text "<exact>" --evidence "<text containing %{error: %{code: …}}>" --yes` printed the success read-back ("the store holds it — criterion index 0"), yet an immediate `bp task get <id> -o json` showed acceptance_criteria[0].met=false and evidence="" on the PUBLISHED row, both before and after `bp task release`. Two attempts with that evidence text were lost the same way (rev 029efed5 -> unchanged). A third attempt on the same row, same epoch flow, same criterion, with the evidence reworded to avoid the `%{` sequence ("code-keyed error maps") persisted (rev 06855830, met=true) and survived release (rev 4190f2fb).

Two hypotheses, not adjudicated here: (a) the evidence string containing `%{` is mangled or dropped somewhere between the CLI and the stored row while the read-back still reports the criterion as held; (b) a rev race between the stamp and the very next write (a pulse or release) reverts the criterion — but the pulse/release ran AFTER the failing read-back in the second attempt too. Either way the stamp's read-back said the store held something the published row did not.

Why it matters: a reconciler stamping evidence that quotes Elixir maps (`%{error: …}`) — the most common shape in this repo's error-envelope rows — gets a green receipt and a row that is still unmet, and nothing downstream says so.

Examples: task-bb83570ba0f6f9f2 crit 0 (lost twice, persisted once reworded). Sibling reads in the same session: one `bp task claim` printed "server error" yet the claim HAD landed (task-96222cef8116f733, epoch 3); `bp task release` after a `bp task pulse` needs the bumped epoch (known, pulse-bumps-the-claim-epoch).

acceptance_criteria.criterion: REPRODUCE OR REFUTE BY RUN on a scratch task: stamp a criterion with --evidence containing the literal sequence %{error: %{code: "x"}} at a held epoch, then read the PUBLISHED row with bp task get -o json; paste both the CLI read-back line and the stored criterion (met, evidence). State which hypothesis holds: evidence text mangled/dropped, or a rev race with the next write.

If reproduced: the stamp read-back is corrected so it reports what the PUBLISHED row holds after the write (met + non-empty evidence), and a regression test pins the %{ evidence case; if refuted: this row closes with the run output and the reworded-evidence coincidence on task-bb83570ba0f6f9f2 explained.

corpus.title: Stamping several criteria in quick succession silently loses evidence — two builders hit it in one wave

content.description:
FILED BY THE WAVE-15 REVIEWER because two independent builders hit the same thing in the same wave and neither filed it.

SYMPTOM, reported identically twice. `bp task stamp … --criterion N --met --evidence '…'` PRINTS a success receipt — cch-w15-s6 quotes '✓ the store holds it — met=true evidence 925 bytes' — and a subsequent `bp task get <id> -o json` reads back met=false with evidence 0B for that same criterion. Both builders caught it ONLY because they re-read the published array; both re-issued the stamp alone and the second attempt persisted.

  - cch-w15-s2-archives-resurrect-scroller, builder review item 7: 'one stamp reported ✓ the store holds it and DID NOT PERSIST (criterion 2 read back met=false)… Anyone trusting the stamp receipt would have shipped an 7/9 board believing it was 8/9.'
  - cch-w15-s6-criteria-amend-by-measurement, builder review item 4: '…most likely the following --miss stamp on criterion 3 wrote back an array it had read before my criterion-2 write. If that is a real read-modify-write race in the stamp merger, other slices stamping several criteria in quick succession are silently losing evidence right now, and nobody would see it.'

WHY THIS IS PRIORITY 1 RATHER THAN A CURIOSITY. This repo's most expensive recurring defect class is a ledger that disagrees with reality (see the false-done and stale-open findings). A stamp verb whose SUCCESS RECEIPT is not evidence of persistence manufactures exactly that divergence, silently, on every wave, and the only reason it was seen at all is that two unusually careful builders re-read. It also directly contradicts the standing rule 'a printed rev is NOT persistence' by making the stamp path look like the one place that rule does not apply.

THE HYPOTHESIS TO TEST FIRST (s6's, quoted rather than adopted): the stamp merger does a read-modify-write of the whole acceptance_criteria array, so a second stamp issued before the first has committed writes back the array it read, erasing the first. If so, --miss is as dangerous as --met, and the window is however long a publish takes.

NOT REPRODUCED DELIBERATELY BY EITHER BUILDER, and not by this reviewer — reproducing it is the first acceptance criterion, not a precondition for filing.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: THE RACE IS REPRODUCED DELIBERATELY: a scripted pair of stamps on two different criteria of one task, issued back to back, is shown losing one of them — with the read-back JSON quoted, and a control (the same two stamps with a wait between) shown persisting both.
THE MECHANISM IS NAMED IN THE CODE, not guessed: the file:line of the read-modify-write (or whatever it actually is) is quoted, and the window is stated.

THE FIX MAKES THE RECEIPT HONEST: either the write is made atomic/CAS-guarded so a lost stamp is impossible, or the verb re-reads and REFUSES with a non-zero exit rather than printing a success line. Proven BY MUTATION — the reproduction from criterion 1 must go from losing a stamp to either persisting both or failing loudly.

corpus.title: bp task stamp --miss is not lossy — the doc's warning was missing and the fleet's bp binary is 3 read-back fixes stale

content.description:
REFUTES the working hypothesis that bp task stamp --miss is conditionally lossy — silently succeeding on a stale or absent claim. Measured against guerrilla on 2026-08-24 with a matrix that reports EXIT CODE and PERSISTENCE separately, because the whole question was whether they ever disagree:

  draft-only-open       exit=6  server=not_in_progress:open  stored=LOST(attempts=0)
  nonholder-inprogress  exit=6  server=not_holder            stored=LOST(attempts=0)
  holder-stale-epoch    exit=6  server=fenced_off            stored=LOST(attempts=0)
  holder-current-epoch  exit=0  server=ok                    stored=PERSISTED

Every refusal is LOUD: non-zero exit, a named error code, and a remedy hint (fenced_off carries 'your claim epoch is stale ... re-claim under your worker id, then retry'). Exit code and persistence agreed in all four cells. The verb is correct.

The API path confirms it by construction: Tasks.Stamp runs check_in_progress -> check_holder -> check_fencing BEFORE any write, and Internal.merge_criteria's miss branch ALWAYS writes both 'attempts' and an explicit 'met'. A miss that reached the merge cannot land without an attempts key — so a stored criterion carrying only [criterion, evidence, met] proves the write never arrived, not that it arrived and was dropped.

A clobber was also considered and REFUTED: all 19 revisions of spd-w18-share-access-btn-names, back to 2026-07-30, show no attempts key on either criterion at any point. Nothing was overwritten; nothing was ever there.

WHAT IS REAL. Two conditions produce the reported symptom, and neither is the verb losing data:
1. A stamp on a DRAFT-ONLY row lands in the store on the draft. bp task get and every board read the PUBLISHED row, so the note is invisible there. The CLI read-back reads the same draft and truthfully reports attempts=1 — a real count of a row nobody reads.
2. The bp binary in fleet use is STALE. Installed: commit dfbb2d929a, built 2026-08-23T17:23Z. git merge-base --is-ancestor proves it contains NONE of 46278e560e (read-back fires on a POST-side 5xx), 46d504424a (the read-back names the row it read — a draft-only stamp stops printing a green), 1c6489c1fb (close and pulse get the same read-back). The second one's subject states the pre-fix behaviour outright: before it, a draft-only stamp DID print a green.

So the fix already landed on main and the fleet is running a binary that predates it. Remedy: make cli-build.

NOT ESTABLISHED, and it is why this row exists rather than a claim of closure: I could not reconstruct which row the original spd-w18 stamp actually hit. Its history carries no attempts at any revision and the row has since been re-claimed and re-opened by another worker, so the state at stamp time is unrecoverable from the ledger. The draft-path explanation FITS every observation but is not PROVEN for that specific row.

Landed in the same pass: docs/setup/TASK-SYSTEM.md gained the warning beside the --miss example, paid for out of existing prose (15978B against a 16000B cap, never raised).

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A CI-runnable regression pins the four-cell exit-vs-persistence matrix (draft-only, non-holder, stale epoch, holder-at-current-epoch) against a live server, so a future change that makes any cell silently succeed REDS. The evidence quotes the run, and the arm is proven able to FAIL by mutation.

The fleet bp binary is proven current: a check reports the installed commit against origin/main HEAD for internal/cli/**, and either the fleet is rebuilt or a staleness warning is emitted where agents will see it. Evidence records the installed commit before and after.

A ruling is recorded on whether a stamp against a draft-only row should REFUSE outright rather than land on the draft and report a truthful green about a row no board reads. If the ruling is refuse, it ships with the remedy in the refusal text; if the ruling is keep, the reason is stated and the CLI warning is verified present in the shipped binary.
The implementing pull request is merged into main, and the criterion evidence records the PR number or merge commit.

corpus.title: bp task close prints 'the store holds it — lifecycle_status=cancelled' for a close that did not persist: the receipt is rendered from the request, not read back

content.description:
MEASURED 2026-09-03T17:1xZ by lead-deploy-3r against guerrilla.barkpark.cloud, with the row id and both receipts kept.

`env -u BARKPARK_TOKEN bp task close dr-w27-instance-serving-since-durable lead-deploy-3 1 cancelled "<reason>" --yes` printed the FULL success receipt:

    ✓ the store holds it — lifecycle_status=cancelled  criteria 0/3 met  claim still held by lead-deploy-3

and `bp task get` seconds later read `lifecycle_status: in_progress`, NO close_reason, and a new rev (34ff9cead4 -> f7ef7a2311). The claim epoch had moved 1 -> 2 (the lane's pulse loop fired between the epoch read and the close). A second close with epoch 2 landed and read back `cancelled` with the reason.

So the receipt's "the store holds it" sentence is rendered from the REQUEST, not from a read-after-write, and a close that lost its CAS (or was superseded) returns exit 0 with the same prose as a close that landed. This is the inverse of the already-documented "close exits non-zero printing stale_claim while the write lands" (LEAD-BRIEF retraction rules): both directions now measured, which means the exit code AND the receipt are uninformative and only a read-back is evidence.

WHO IS MISLED: every scripted close/stamp in the campaign that trusts the receipt — a lead trims the row from its pulse list on the receipt, the claim lapses 40 min later, the row reads open again with nobody holding it.

The same shape almost certainly applies to `bp task stamp` ("the store holds it — met=true" with a later read of met=false is already in the memory of two leads).

acceptance_criteria.criterion: bp task close and bp task stamp render their success line ONLY from a read-after-write of the row (or from the server response echoing the persisted lifecycle_status / criterion met+evidence), never from the request; a close whose read-back does not show the requested lifecycle_status exits non-zero and names what the row actually reads

MUTATION-PROVED: a Go test drives close against a fake server that ACCEPTS the request but persists nothing (or persists a different lifecycle) and asserts a non-zero exit with the observed lifecycle in the message; the same test red on origin/main is pasted

The server-side cause of the accepted-but-not-persisted close is named (CAS loss on a moved epoch returning 2xx, a superseding write, or a stale read replica) with a reproduction, or the row states it could not be reproduced and why

corpus.title: A stamp whose own read-back said 'the store holds it' was found reverted one write later — observed once in ~20 writes, not reproduced

content.description:
OBSERVED LIVE during cch-w16-s5 on 2026-08-01, and it QUALIFIES that same slice's cancellation of cch-w15-bl-stamp-merger-silently-drops-evidence and pds-bl-task-stamp-silent-nonland — so it is filed rather than swallowed.

SEQUENCE, exactly as it happened on cch-w12-bl-filing-law-parent-charter-half (epoch 1, worker epic-builder-the-ledger-stops-lying-in-both-direction):
  1. stamp --criterion 0 --met  -> printed the #8281 client read-back line: 'the store holds it — criterion index 0 (#1 as boards number them): met=true evidence 2114 bytes'.
  2. stamp --criterion 1 --met  -> printed 'the store holds it — criterion index 1 (#2 as boards number them): met=true evidence 1981 bytes'.
  3. stamp --criterion 2 --miss --note '...'  -> printed 'the store holds it — criterion index 2: met=false ... attempts=1'.
  4. INDEPENDENT re-read (bp task get -o json, fresh process): criterion 0 met=true 2102 chars, criterion 1 met=FALSE evidence LENGTH 0, criterion 2 met=false with the note present. Lifecycle 1/3.
Criterion 1's met flag and its ~2 kB of evidence were GONE, one write after a receipt that explicitly claimed the store held them.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT ESTABLISHED. Re-issuing the criterion-1 stamp landed it (2/3, verified by a fresh read). A DELIBERATE control then re-ran the same --miss on criterion 2 with the row quiescent, and it did NOT revert criterion 1 — so a naive 'the --miss path does a whole-array read-modify-write' story is REFUTED as stated. One occurrence in roughly twenty ledger writes in that run; the same run twice hit 'context deadline exceeded' on /v1/capabilities and once a 500 on /v1/data/mutate under its own headless-Chrome load, which is the alternative explanation pds-bl-task-stamp-silent-nonland already names.

WHY IT IS PRIORITY 1 ANYWAY. The whole point of the #8281 read-back is that a printed receipt means the store holds it. Here the receipt said exactly that and the value was gone at the next read. If the loss is real, the read-back is not a sufficient guarantee and every 'stamped and verified' criterion in every epic is one write away from being unaudited. If the loss is a read-back artefact (a stale replica answering the post-write read), that is a different bug in the same instrument and equally worth naming. Either way the only thing that CAUGHT it was a second, independent read from a fresh process — which is why the one-at-a-time re-read discipline stays law.

RELATION TO THE TWO ROWS CANCELLED IN THE SAME RUN: those cancellations stand on their own stated grounds — the publish-door erasure was real, was fixed by 71a177742 (#8283) and was driven here to a live 422; and no scripted stamp PAIR has ever been shown losing a write across five experiments. This row does not resurrect either premise. It records a THIRD, narrower observation that neither of them predicted, so the ledger does not have to remember it as folklore.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: THE LOSS IS REPRODUCED OR REFUTED ON PURPOSE: a scripted sequence of N met-stamps followed by a --miss is run M times against one throwaway task, each step followed by an INDEPENDENT read from a fresh process, and the observed loss rate is stated with N and M. A run that never loses one is a REFUTATION and must say so.

THE READ-BACK IS TESTED AS A WITNESS, not trusted: it is shown either that the post-write read hits the same row the write hit, or that it can be answered by a stale view — with the code path quoted at file:line.

IF THE LOSS IS REAL, the receipt stops claiming what it cannot know: the verb refuses or warns with a non-zero exit rather than printing a success line, proven by mutation against the pre-fix behaviour.

THE OBSERVATION IS REACHABLE FROM THE TWO ROWS IT QUALIFIES: cch-w15-bl-stamp-merger-silently-drops-evidence and pds-bl-task-stamp-silent-nonland are both named in the finding, and the verdict states whether either cancellation was wrong.

corpus.title: bp task close reports stale_claim (rc=6) for a close whose write LANDED — the already-terminal guard is not idempotent for the same closer

content.description: MEASURED 2026-09-02 by lead-triage-o: five closes each exited rc=6 printing stale_claim while the row was in fact closed, each stored with its own close reason verbatim. The natural recovery makes it worse — a re-claim then fails not_ready because the row is already closed — so a worker that trusts the exit code reports a correctly-closed row as uncloseable, and the campaign's interim rule became 'read back before believing a bp write FAILED', which is a workaround, not a fix. MECHANISM, located on origin/main: api/lib/barkpark/tasks/close.ex line ~392, inside the per-task advisory lock. When no explicit observed_rev is passed and the row is ALREADY in a terminal lifecycle, close returns {:error, :stale_claim} unconditionally. That guard is correct for a genuine lost race between two DIFFERENT closers — without it the default-observed-rev CAS would let every caller succeed in turn. It is wrong for a RETRY by the SAME closer: attempt 1 commits, the response is lost or times out under load, attempt 2 reads the now-terminal row and is told the write failed. Under this campaign's measured load (429s and DB pool saturation on the same ledger) a slow first response tripping a client retry is the ordinary case, not an exotic one. THE SHAPE OF THE FIX: make the already-terminal arm IDEMPOTENT when the stored close attributes name the SAME worker closing to the SAME lifecycle — return the stored row as a success receipt that says plainly it was already closed, rather than a failure. A terminal row closed by ANYONE ELSE, or to a different status, must keep returning stale_claim: that is a real lost race and the caller must hear about it. Do not widen the CAS, and do not make close unconditionally idempotent.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: REPRODUCED BY TEST on today's main: a second close by the SAME worker, same target lifecycle, no explicit observed_rev, against a row that first close already committed, returns {:error, :stale_claim}. The test reds before the fix. Evidence: the red run output.

After the fix that same second close returns a SUCCESS receipt carrying the stored row, and the receipt states that the row was already closed rather than pretending this call closed it. The stored close_reason, claim.closed_by and claim.closed_at are byte-unchanged by the second call — asserted directly, since a second close silently overwriting the first reason would trade one lie for another.

THE RACE IS STILL REFUSED: a terminal row closed by a DIFFERENT worker, and a terminal row closed to a DIFFERENT lifecycle, both still return stale_claim. Both cases tested, because an idempotency that cannot tell a retry from a lost race is worse than the bug.
MUTATION-PROVED: disarm the fix and the new tests red again; disarm only the same-worker predicate and the race tests go green (proving they actually discriminate). Runs captured and reverted.

The bp CLI exit code follows the server: the idempotent second close exits 0, not 6. Demonstrated end to end against a dev server, with the transcript. If the Go side needs a change it is named for the CLI lane rather than made here.
MERGE-GATED (the lead closes this): PR merged to main with the required gates green on its head, merge sha recorded.

corpus.title: A single `bp task stamp --miss` landed TWICE, 1.9 s apart, and returned rc=0 once — a retry of a write that had already succeeded is invisible to the caller

content.description:
MEASURED 2026-09-07T18:20Z by lead-ledger-c4 while stamping pdf-w1-secure-stall-diagnosis. Found by reading the row back after writing, not by any error.

WHAT HAPPENED. One python script wrote three stamps in a loop over one claim epoch: c1 --met, c0 --miss, c2 --miss. Each bp invocation returned rc=0 exactly once. Reading the row back, c0 carried TWO attempts, c2 carried ONE.

THE TWO c0 ATTEMPTS ARE IDENTICAL: same worker (lead-ledger-c4), same 1,167-character note, byte for byte. Their timestamps are 2026-09-07T18:20:03.575379Z and 2026-09-07T18:20:05.482392Z.

THE TIMESTAMPS ARE THE DISCRIMINATOR AND THEY RULE OUT THE INNOCENT EXPLANATION. 1.9 SECONDS APART is not a single handler appending twice - that would produce identical or sub-millisecond timestamps. It is the shape of a CLIENT RETRY of a request that had already been applied server-side: the first attempt landed and its response was lost or timed out, the client retried, the second landed too, and the caller saw only the second one's rc=0.

WHY IT MATTERS EVEN THOUGH THIS INSTANCE WAS HARMLESS. Here the target was an append-only attempts[] list and the two entries are identical, so nothing was corrupted and nothing was lost. But the caller CANNOT SEE THE DUPLICATE - a retry that succeeds is indistinguishable from a first attempt that succeeded. The same retry against a verb whose effect is not idempotent is a silent double-apply. `bp task pulse` ADVANCES THE CLAIM EPOCH on every call, and the campaign's whole stamp/close protocol is a CAS on that epoch, so a retried pulse moves the epoch twice while the caller believes it moved once - and the next stamp or close then fails a CAS the operator has no way to explain.

THIS IS THE CAMPAIGN'S RECURRING SHAPE, INVERTED. Most of the instrument faults measured this week are a failed read rendering as an empty result. This is a SUCCEEDED WRITE rendering as a single write. Both are the caller being unable to tell what actually happened from what it was told.

NOT MEASURED, AND SAID RATHER THAN GUESSED: I did not reproduce it deliberately, I do not know the trigger (a slow response? a 5xx? a transport reset?), and I did not check whether the retry is in `bp`'s HTTP client, in a wrapper, or in the server. One occurrence out of three writes in one script is the whole sample. The rate is UNKNOWN, not low.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: THE RETRY IS LOCATED AND NAMED: state where the second request comes from - bp's HTTP client, a wrapper, or a server-side replay - with the file:line that issues it. Reproduce it deliberately (an injected slow or failed response on a write that the server nevertheless applies) rather than waiting for it to recur, and quote the run. If it CANNOT be reproduced, say UNCONFIRMED and do not close on that - a non-reproduction from a non-exhaustive search is not a refutation.

A RETRIED WRITE THAT ALREADY LANDED IS EITHER PREVENTED OR MADE VISIBLE. Either the write carries an idempotency key so the second application is a no-op, or the caller is told the response was a replay. A silent second apply is the defect; a second apply the caller can SEE is acceptable. Prove it on the two verbs where it costs most: `bp task stamp --miss` (append-only, this instance) and `bp task pulse` (ADVANCES THE CLAIM EPOCH, so a double-apply desynchronises the CAS that every stamp and close depends on).

NON-VACUITY, required, because this whole row is about a check that cannot see what it is looking for: the guard must be shown to FAIL when the protection is removed. Mutate away the idempotency key or the replay signal and show the duplicate returns, with the mutation PROVEN TO HAVE APPLIED (anchor matches exactly once, non-empty diff, still compiles). A test that passes both with and without the fix is measuring nothing.

corpus.title: bp task stamp printed "the store holds it - met=true" for two criteria and the store did not hold either

content.description:
MEASURED 2026-09-02 22:40Z by lead-silent on task-bf35709acc546392, on the live guerrilla ledger.

WHAT HAPPENED. Two `bp task stamp --met` calls each printed the success receipt:
  "the store holds it - criterion index 2 (#3 as boards number them): met=true  evidence 999 bytes ..."
  "the store holds it - criterion index 3 (#4 as boards number them): met=true  evidence 1409 bytes ..."
A `bp task get` seconds later, and again minutes later, showed BOTH criteria met=false with evidence of ZERO bytes. The writes never landed. The receipt says "the store holds it" and the store did not hold it.

HOW IT SURFACED, which is the only reason it was caught at all: the following `bp task close` refused with "acceptance criteria 2, 3 (0-BASED) are not met on the task AS STORED". Had that row carried no close-time criteria gate, or had I closed with an override, two criteria would have read MET on a board while carrying no evidence at all. The receipt is not evidence; the read-back is.

WHAT IT IS NOT. I tested the obvious candidate and cleared it: a DELIBERATELY stale epoch is LOUD. Stamping with epoch 1 while the claim sat higher printed "hint: your claim epoch is stale - most often your own bp task pulse bumped it ... re-read claim.epoch and retry" and wrote nothing. So the stale-epoch path refuses honestly and does not explain a success receipt over a missing write.

RELATED OBSERVATION, possibly the same root: on this row `bp task get` intermittently returns content.claim.epoch = null and claim.worker = null WHILE lifecycle_status reads in_progress and the holder can still stamp. A caller that re-reads claim.epoch to satisfy the stale-epoch hint above can therefore read null, and any parser doing .get("epoch") on it gets nothing to pass back.

WHO IS MISLED AND WHAT THEY WRONGLY CONCLUDE. Every lead and worker in this campaign records proof through stamp and reads its receipt as confirmation. They conclude a criterion carries evidence when it carries none. Evidence is PERMANENT at close, so a row can be sealed asserting a criterion was proven with an empty evidence field.

SMALLEST CHANGE THAT MAKES IT LOUD: the stamp receipt must be rendered FROM THE STORED DOCUMENT after the write, not from the request that was sent. If the write did not land, print a refusal naming the criterion index. Until then the operational rule is: never trust a stamp receipt - re-read the row and confirm met and evidence length before you close.

REPRODUCTION IS NOT YET RELIABLE. I hit it twice in one command and could not reproduce it deliberately afterwards; re-stamping the same two criteria against a freshly re-claimed epoch persisted and read back correctly. Filing it with the measurement rather than a mechanism, because a receipt that can lie about a durable write is worth knowing about even unexplained.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The stamp receipt is rendered FROM THE STORED DOCUMENT after the write, not from the request that was sent. Proved by mutation: make the write fail (or drop it) and show the command prints a refusal naming the criterion index instead of 'the store holds it'.

A read-back assertion exists in the write path or the CLI: after a --met stamp, the criterion's stored met flag and evidence LENGTH are confirmed non-empty before the success line prints. A zero-byte evidence field on a met=true criterion is refused.

content.claim.epoch no longer reads null while lifecycle_status is in_progress and the holder can still stamp — or, if that shape is legitimate, the stale-epoch hint stops telling callers to re-read a field that can be null, and names what to do instead.

Whether or not the root cause is found, the operational rule is written into the task-system doc and the campaign brief: a stamp receipt is not evidence, re-read the row and confirm met plus evidence length before closing. Quote the added lines.

corpus.title: bp task stamp can return exit 0 on a write that never lands

content.description:
PROVEN BY OBSERVATION DURING WAVE 25, and it is the epic's own class of defect turned inward: a verb that says it did something it did not do, inside the ledger writer every other proof in this epic rests on.

WHAT HAPPENED. The pds-w25-census-clause-4 builder issued 'bp task stamp' for criterion 3 with an evidence string of roughly 1.1 kB. The command returned EXIT 0 and the normal help envelope — no error, no truncation warning, no partial receipt. A read-back of the row showed met:false and evidence:"". The write was silently DROPPED, not rejected. A re-issue with a shorter string landed; a 950-char re-issue also landed, which points at a size-related ceiling somewhere in the stamp path rather than at transient server load, though load cannot be excluded (guerrilla was intermittently 500ing on /v1/data/mutate and /v1/capabilities during the same window while /v1/tasks stamp+pulse kept answering).

WHY IT IS PRIORITY 1. Every acceptance criterion in this epic — and the whole 'read the field back and COUNT it' doctrine — assumes that a stamp which returns success has persisted. If it can return success without persisting, then any wave that batched its stamps and did not re-read has an unknown number of phantom-met criteria, and the sibling-epic finding where 45 claimed parks re-derived to ZERO is exactly the shape this would produce.

WHY IT WAS NOT FILED WHEN FOUND. The builder tried five consecutive times and guerrilla returned internal_error / client timeout on every attempt (request_ids GMcnFGWz9awWmRgAAn7R, GMcnJZ5I77RLPAIAAsZR, GMcnMgX6UvldJdgAAzgx, GMcnTR_60BgHcd0AA9Xx). The finding lived only in the builder report and on the claim now-line until the wave reviewer filed it here.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT. Find the size or encoding boundary at which a stamp is dropped; make the drop a REFUSAL with a named error rather than a success; and add a regression that stamps an oversized evidence string and asserts either persistence or a non-zero exit — never exit 0 with an empty field.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The boundary is identified by bisection: the smallest evidence payload that returns exit 0 and does NOT persist is named with its byte size, and the largest that does persist is named beside it
A stamp that cannot persist its evidence returns a NON-ZERO exit with a named error code; exit 0 with an unwritten field is impossible on any path
A regression test stamps an over-boundary evidence string and asserts persistence-or-refusal; the test is mutation-proven to fail against the pre-fix behaviour
The read-back-and-count doctrine is either vindicated or amended in the charter based on what the bisection finds

corpus.title: The GitHub bridge stamps synced_rev pointing at a revision that was discarded, and a lost backlink orphans an issue

content.description:
TWO DEFECTS FOUND BY A/B PROBE THIS WAVE, both on the epic's own law (a receipt lies when the value it emits does not descend from the write return).

(1) SYNCED_REV NAMES A REVISION THAT NO LONGER EXISTS. `bp doc discard-draft task <id>` returned rc=0 and, 440 ms later, three phantom history rows appeared (discardDraft, create, publish). The publish revision afcafb30-d8a9-47f8-b23e-72488b36a35f carries `github: {issue: 9307, state: "synced", synced_rev: "e1655bcc5a6f83d03758c66fb7e5c870"}` -- and e1655bcc is EXACTLY the _rev the discard receipt had just reported for the draft it removed. The mirror claims it synced a revision that was discarded.

(2) A PATCH ON A PUBLISHED TASK ORPHANS ITS ISSUE. `bp doc patch <published-task-id>` mints a draft twin that CAPTURES the github writeback, so the PUBLISHED row never learns its issue number. A probe row ended with `github: None` at lifecycle cancelled while GitHub issue 9306 stayed OPEN rendering `- [ ] criterion C two` against a task holding met:true. A close does not propagate through a lost backlink. (Five sibling probes' closes DID propagate within ~50 s; this one did not and was closed by hand.)

(3) RELATED, ALREADY FILED, DO NOT REFILE: an unpublished task edit AUTO-PUBLISHES itself within about 40 seconds with no publish issued by anyone (Link.put's draft-twin collapse) -- pds-bl-github-linkput-auto-publish-erasure and cch-w12-bl-mirror-syncs-unpublished-drafts. Wave 26's erasure fence DOES hold (publishing a stale twin over landed stamps is refused rc=5 validation_failed); the auto-publish itself still happens. A type:task DRAFT IS NOT A STAGING STATE -- any check that patches a draft and inspects it before it goes live has ~40 seconds.

(4) THE MIRROR EATS THROWAWAYS: six scratch rows minted six real public GitHub issues, INCLUDING one for a row that never published. Any fixture or gate that creates task rows creates public issues.

Both (1) and (2) were observed n=1 on a live shared ledger under concurrent wave load. A clean two-task A/B is the first work here.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Defect (1) is reproduced or refuted by a clean two-task A/B on a quiet ledger -- evidence quotes the discard receipt's _rev beside the subsequent revision's synced_rev.

Defect (2) is reproduced or refuted: a bp doc patch on a published task either preserves the published row's github pointer, or the row states exactly where the writeback lands -- evidence quotes the published row's github field before and after.
If confirmed, synced_rev is made to descend from the write that actually landed, and a fix or a named refusal is recorded -- evidence quotes the shipped behaviour.
If confirmed, a task close propagates to its issue even after a draft twin captured the backlink, or the failure mode is documented with its detection -- evidence quotes an issue state after a close.
MERGE-GATED: merged to main with its gates green, or the row is closed as REFUTED with the A/B output attached.

corpus.title: bp task stamp --criterion N is 0-INDEXED while every board/rubric renders criteria 1..N — a builder stamping 1..N silently flips the wrong criterion (incl. merge-gated ones)

content.description:
HIT LIVE while building site-spawner-w3-admin-site-deploy-seam (2026-07-14).

`bp task stamp <id> <worker> <epoch> --criterion N` treats N as a 0-BASED index into acceptance_criteria. But bp task get, the rubric, the spawn prompts, and every board render criteria as 1..N. A builder who follows the visible numbering therefore attaches EVERY evidence string to the criterion one slot LATER than intended.

Why it is worse than a cosmetic off-by-one: on a 7-criterion task whose #7 is the standard '[MERGE-GATED — the lead closes this]' criterion, a builder stamping 1..6 flips criteria 2..7 — which MARKS THE MERGE-GATED CRITERION MET before the PR even exists. The builder contract explicitly forbids that, and the ledger is what the lead trusts at merge. It also means five criteria carry evidence that does not describe them, which is exactly the false-done fabrication class the ledger exists to prevent.

I only caught it by dumping evidence-vs-criterion pairs after stamping; nothing in the CLI's output hints at it (each stamp returns a bare 'epoch=N rev=...'). --miss cannot un-flip a lock, so recovery needs a raw bp doc patch of the whole acceptance_criteria array + re-publish.

FIX (pick one, do not do both silently): (a) make --criterion 1-based to match every surface — the least-surprise option, but it is a breaking change for any script already passing 0-based; or (b) keep 0-based and make the CLI ECHO what it stamped ('criterion 3/7: "<first 60 chars>" -> met') so a mis-index is visible in one line. (b) is worth doing REGARDLESS of (a): a stamp that does not name what it stamped cannot be audited.

Guard: refuse --met on a criterion whose text contains 'MERGE-GATED' unless an explicit --merge-gated override is passed. That is a cheap tripwire on the one flip that actually corrupts a lead's merge decision.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: bp task stamp --criterion N is unambiguous: either 1-based to match every rendering surface, or documented 0-based AND the CLI echoes the criterion text it stamped so a mis-index is visible immediately.
A regression test proves that stamping the criteria a builder SEES (1..N) lands each evidence string on the criterion it describes.
--met on a criterion whose text contains MERGE-GATED is refused without an explicit override, so a builder cannot pre-flip the leads merge gate.

corpus.title: bp manifest dispatch has no transient-500 retry: every task verb hard-fails on the first internal_error while the capabilities fetch alone retries

content.description: TRAP HIT BY lead-console and three of its workers on 2026-09-01/02: guerrilla's task routes return internal_error on roughly a third of calls during the campaign (the incident task-d89e42ea727bffb7 names), and bp turns EACH one into a hard failure — bp task get, claim, stamp, close, ls --all every one of them died on the first 500 and had to be wrapped in shell retry loops by hand. Meanwhile bp already prints 'transient internal_error from GET /v1/capabilities — retrying (attempt 1 of 3)': internal/apiclient/retry.go carries a narrow GET-only internal_error retry that ONLY the capabilities fetch uses. internal/cli/run.go doRequestCT (the manifest dispatch every verb rides) uses a bare http.Client with no retry at all. THE FIX: route manifest dispatch through the same bounded retry for IDEMPOTENT requests — GET/HEAD always; a write ONLY when the verb is CAS-fenced or otherwise safe to repeat (claim, pulse, stamp and close are epoch/rev-fenced so a duplicate cannot double-apply — say per verb why it is safe, and leave create/mutate un-retried because a 500 can be a write-then-error). Same backoff and attempt cap as the capabilities path, one stderr line per retry, and a final failure that names the request_id of the LAST attempt. Also: bp task ls --all / --match must retry a failed PAGE in place, and a page that still fails after the cap is a named refusal, never a shorter list presented as complete. Fence: internal/cli (run.go + task verbs), internal/apiclient/retry.go; Go tests against an httptest server that 500s N-1 times then 200s, and one that 500s every time and asserts the named refusal + request_id.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: GET/HEAD manifest dispatches retry a transient internal_error with the same bounded backoff the capabilities fetch uses, print one stderr line per retry, and the final failure names the last request_id — proven by a Go test with an httptest server that 500s twice then 200s, and one that 500s every time.

For each write verb that is retried (claim, pulse, stamp, close at minimum) the PR states why a repeat cannot double-apply (the epoch/rev CAS), and create/mutate-style writes are NOT retried; a test proves a fenced write retried after a 500 lands exactly once.
bp task ls --all (and --match) retries a failed page in place and refuses by name if a page still fails after the cap, never printing a partial list as complete — proven by a paged httptest fixture.

corpus.title: The LEAD stamps 0-9 from the one transcript, then 10 on merge, then 11 alone

content.description:
AFTER pds-w13-crown-climb AND pds-w13-charter-lands MERGE.

STAMP THE CROWN FROM THE ONE TRANSCRIPT. This is the LEAD's job and no builder may do it alongside the rung it just ran. It is ROUND 2 and dispatches only once both dependencies are ON MAIN.

SCOPE IS ALL ELEVEN, and there is no run-invariant subset to carry forward (PDS-D234). Every one of criteria 0-9 is a claim about what a run did or what a transcript says, in run-indexed language its authors chose deliberately ("re-derived at RUN TIME", "the run output is pasted", "the run's OWN measured RSS peak", "the run kept PDS_STEP5_FAILDEMO=1"). Zero make a run-invariant structural claim. Do not spend time hunting for a subset -- it is not there.
Criterion 0 is the quietest trap: it is the ONLY met criterion naming a run, so a stamper may leave it alone -- but its claim is about the DEPLOYED SHA, which has moved to 859c137cd. It is stale in SUBSTANCE, not merely in attribution. Re-stamp it.
Criterion 6 is the inverse trap: it reads met=FALSE while its evidence NAMES a run id (wave 7's, where rung 6 FAILED). Key on the `met` flag, NEVER on run-id presence.

ORDER, and it is not negotiable:
 1. Criteria 0-9, each citing the fresh RUN_ID from the committed transcript.
 2. Criterion 10 LAST of the run-bearing set, on merge, carrying the SAME run id as a POINTER (its own text requires rungs 3+4 green "in the transcript of the wave that pays this criterion").
 3. Criterion 11 ALONE and LAST, only after verifying the eleven ids are byte-identical. Its met-flip removes the final brake on the cmux Stop-hook auto-close.

MECHANICS (PDS-D226 -- uniform fetch-to-file for ALL TWELVE, no per-criterion judgement). Use scripts/pds-crown-stamp.sh, which is on main. NEVER type criterion text inline: criterion 6 carries 8 backticks that the shell runs as command substitution (and `command` is a zsh BUILTIN, so one of its four pairs mangles with NO "command not found" line), and c5/c6/c11 carry single quotes -- criterion 11 carries exactly ONE in 1248 characters, invisible on inspection, stamped last at maximum fatigue. Fetch each criterion's exact stored text to a file via a JSON-field write and pass --criterion-text "$(cat f)". Indices are ZERO-BASED (PDS-D149).
Keep evidence TERSE -- run id plus transcript pointer. The request target must stay <= 9984 bytes (Bandit max_request_line_length 10000); per-criterion budgets run 7197 (c6, tightest) to 9759 (c3), and a good stamp spends well under 1%. Oversized stamps are fail-closed, so recovery is "retry shorter", never "reconcile a half-write".
If a stamp is REJECTED, check the claim epoch FIRST -- `bp task pulse` bumps it and a stamp using the claim-time epoch gets fenced out. Re-claim and re-read the epoch.

WHAT MAY HONESTLY BE ASSERTED (PDS-D236): "Rung N passed under run <id>, as recorded in that run's own summary roster in scripts/pds-pull-proof.crown-transcript-w13.txt, a transcript whose banner and summary both carry <id> and which prints the unqualified RESULT: PASS line the harness emits only when all rungs ran in one process." If the climb embedded $RUN_TAG per PDS-D233, add that the rung bodies cite the cksum of that run id. Do NOT claim each rung body is individually in-band tokened -- without the RUN_TAG embedding, attribution is process-level, not rung-level.

IF THE CLIMB REFUSED. Stamp NOTHING. A partial run re-stamped over wave-7 evidence would strictly DESTROY information. Record the refusal, leave every criterion as it stands, and file the successor.

corpus.title: bp task pulse returns rc=0 + epoch on a row that is NOT in_progress — a green pulse log is not evidence of a claim

content.description:
A GREEN PULSE LOG IS NOT EVIDENCE OF A CLAIM. Measured 2026-09-06 by lead-cli-5 on two rows in one hour, and the same misreading cost the orchestrator an hour across three lanes the same morning.

WHAT HAPPENED. task-ee33b6f088b35bdb and task-8f9d3ea8926f387f both read `lifecycle_status: open` with `claim.worker: lead-cli` still set (epochs 8 and 4) while the lane's pulse loop had logged `ok … epoch=N` on them every 15-minute cycle up to 06:28:54Z. `bp task stamp` then refused: "this row is open, not in_progress — a stamp writes under a LIVE claim". A fresh `bp task claim` (epoch bumped to 9 / 5) fixed it. Two other rows (task-e49058a7f2b46a63, task-650d7844d8fe7199) read open with `claim: null` — the ordinary lapse. So there are at least TWO shapes a lapsed row takes, and only one of them clears `claim.worker`.

WHY IT IS A HOLE. `bp task pulse <id> <worker> --now … --yes` returned rc=0 and printed `epoch=N` on rows that were not in_progress. Every keep-alive loop in the campaign treats that rc=0 as "the claim is held" (that is the loop's only success signal, and its 3-strike alarm keys on refusals). A pulse that succeeds on a row the ledger no longer considers claimed makes the loop's liveness AND its log both say "held" while the next stamp/close fails. Cross-reference pds-bl-null-expiry-claims-repo-wide: 6,850 of 8,617 open rows carry a claim object (median age 27 days) and 63 of the 1,000 `bp task ready` rows still carry one — `claim.worker` and the row's actual state are loosely coupled, and pulse is the seam where a loop gets told the wrong thing.

WHAT TO ESTABLISH FIRST (read the writer, do not guess): (a) what `bp task pulse` / POST pulse does on a row whose lifecycle_status is not in_progress — does it bump the epoch, refresh a lease, or no-op — and what it returns; (b) which server path takes a row from in_progress back to open while LEAVING claim.worker set (lease sweeper? a `stage` transition? a publish of a stale draft twin? the 2026-09-06 rows had draft twins discarded that day); (c) whether the lapse sweeper is expected to clear claim.worker and did not.

THE INVARIANT (mechanism is the builder's): a pulse on a row that is not in_progress is a REFUSAL that names the row's actual state, never rc=0 with an epoch — so a keep-alive loop's success signal cannot lie about the claim. A pulse on an in_progress row held by another worker stays refused as today (not_holder).

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Reproduced on a throwaway row: claim it, take it out of in_progress by the same path the 2026-09-06 rows took (established by reading the code, not assumed), then `bp task pulse` — the rc, the printed epoch line, and the row's lifecycle_status + claim.worker read back are pasted. Probe row cancelled afterwards with a reason naming this row.

Server-side: a pulse on a row whose lifecycle_status is not in_progress is REFUSED with an error naming the actual state and the fix (`bp task claim`); a pulse on a held in_progress row by its holder still succeeds; a pulse by a non-holder stays refused as today. A test per arm; the refusal test shown RED before the change (mutation asserted applied).

The path that leaves claim.worker set on an open row is named from the code, and either fixed (the lapse clears the stale claim, test-pinned) or explicitly recorded as intended with the reason and a cross-reference to pds-bl-null-expiry-claims-repo-wide.

content.description:
PREREQUISITE OF THE GREEN, not a backlog nicety (charter PDS-D196). Crown criterion 10's stored text
says it is "NOT to be stamped until rungs 3 and 4 are GREEN in the wave-9 transcript". That transcript
is scripts/pds-pull-proof.crown-transcript-w8.txt — committed, APPEND-ONLY per its own header at :3,
and recording rungs 3 and 4 as ABORT at :322/:324 forever.

letter-of-the-law escape, appending wave 10's run into the wave-9 file, produces ONE file carrying TWO
run ids for a reader to stitch — exactly what criterion 11 exists to forbid. That escape is REFUSED.

and leave this criterion unmet"), so it blocks ONLY the green. If the climb fires green and this has

Land a record of the amendment in scripts/pds-crown-ledger-w10-amendment.md (a NEW file — do NOT touch
scripts/pds-crown-ledger-2026-07-20.md, a sibling slice owns it) carrying the before and after text of

corpus.title: bp task stamp's read-back cannot name the row it read, so a draft-only stamp prints a green that the board never shows

content.description:
PROVEN BY RUN THIS WAVE. `bp task stamp` DOES have a read-back (PDS-D359/D361) and it fires -- but internal/apiclient/client.go:1305-1311 decodes an envelope of exactly `{ok, reason, doc:{content}}`, throwing away `doc.status` and `doc.doc_id` -- the only two fields carrying draft/publish truth. They never reach taskboard.FetchCriterion (internal/taskboard/criterion_readback.go:33) or renderStampVerdict.

CONSEQUENCE: GET /v1/tasks/:doc_id falls back to the `drafts.` twin when no published row exists, so stamping a criterion on a draft-only task -- exactly what `bp task create --yes` produces at rc=0 -- makes the read-back read the DRAFT, find the criterion it just wrote, and print the green verdict. The value LANDED; the board never shows the row. Verified: a draft-only stamp printed 'the store holds it' at rc=0 with criteria_progress {met:1,total:1} on drafts.pds-w43-verify-probe-*, while `bp doc get task <id>` returned rc=4 not_found.

A CODE COMMENT IS REFUTED BY RUN: internal/cli/tasks_stamp_cmd.go:158-163 asserts "the read-back always sees the row bp task stamp wrote, which is the PUBLISHED one (PDS-D360)". On a draft-only row there IS no published row.

THE FIX IS ~6 LINES IN TWO FILES: add Status and DocID to TaskGetContent's decode struct and have the verdict renderer refuse a green when doc_id starts with "drafts." (or status != "published"). Testable by substitution: feed it a drafts. doc_id and the receipt must go non-zero.

NOTE the residual exposure errs the OTHER way and is separate: if a row is draft-only at write time and gets published between write and read-back, the read-back reads the published row -- a false RED. That window is not hypothetical (see the auto-publish backlog row).

Surface: Go CLI. Gate: CC=clang go build ./... && go vet ./internal/cli/... && go test ./internal/cli/...

acceptance_criteria.criterion: TaskGetContent decodes doc.status and doc.doc_id and passes them to the verdict renderer -- evidence quotes the new struct and the call chain.
A stamp whose read-back lands on a drafts. row exits NON-ZERO with a message naming the draft, instead of printing the green verdict -- evidence quotes the receipt and the exit code from a run.
MUTATION: reverting the doc_id check makes the new test RED -- evidence quotes the failing assertion.
The false comment at internal/cli/tasks_stamp_cmd.go:158-163 is corrected to match the world -- evidence quotes old and new.
GATE GREEN: CC=clang go build ./... && go vet ./internal/cli/... && go test ./internal/cli/... -- evidence quotes rc=0 and the test summary.

corpus.title: bp task claim hides the lease, and pulse silently invalidates the epoch the help says to keep

(1) `bp task claim <id> <worker> --yes` prints help lines carrying the epoch but NOTHING about lease length or expiry; a lead that claimed four rows at 21:50Z and dispatched builders found at 22:31Z that the claim on cch-w34-bl-false-open-sweep-instrument-fails-silent-empty had lapsed 29s before its PR opened, so the pr-task-gate refused PR #14866 and `bp task next` handed a sibling row (cchi-w62-…) to another lead mid-build. corpus.title: bp task create --yes prints a draft receipt at rc=0 and the row never reaches the board

content.description:
FOUND BY THE FIRST REAL USER OF THE WAVE-28 BIRTH-FENCE REGIME (wave 29, the pds-w29-write-receipt-fence builder), reported in that task's ledger and folded into the wave-29 debrief.

Measured, live, under wave load: `bp task create --yes ...` returned {"draft":"drafts.pds-w29-...","status":"draft"} at rc=0 and the task was NOT published. corpus.title: The crown stamp becomes a scripted, rehearsed operation instead of twelve chances to mangle a criterion

content.description:
ROUND 1 - dependency-free, builds now. Touches no file any other slice touches.

When the climb greens, twelve criteria get stamped under fatigue, and a mangled stamp after a successful climb is unrecoverable in the moment. Both halves of the recipe were already PROVEN live against a disposable scratch task; this slice turns that proof into a committed tool.

WHAT WAS PROVEN. (a) Pasting criterion 6 inline into a double-quoted shell string ran its four backtick pairs as command substitution; the server rejected the stamp with criteria_mismatch, exit 2, NOTHING written. (b) --criterion-text with $(cat c6.txt) and the identical 2490-char text stamped clean, exit 0.

DELIVER scripts/pds-crown-stamp.sh: fetch criterion N's EXACT stored wording from the server to a file via a JSON-field write (python or jq), then stamp passing the file's contents by command substitution. Never a here-doc and never an echo - command substitution strips ALL trailing newlines, and this recipe is safe only because 0 of the 12 crown criteria carry trailing whitespace today, i.e. safe by luck of the data, not by construction. A JSON-field write keeps it that way.

THE LAW IS UNIFORM FETCH-TO-FILE FOR ALL TWELVE (PDS-D226), no per-criterion judgement. Criterion 6 is the only one of twelve unsafe in a double-quoted string (8 backticks) and it fails LOUDLY - but c5, c6 and c11 all carry single quotes, and CRITERION 11 CARRIES EXACTLY ONE IN 1248 CHARACTERS. It is invisible on inspection, it is stamped LAST and ALONE at maximum fatigue, and its met-flip removes the final brake on the cmux Stop-hook auto-close. Uniform law exists precisely so nobody eyeballs c11, sees no backticks, and types it inline. Note also that 'command' is a zsh BUILTIN, so of criterion 6's four backtick pairs only three emit 'command not found' - the fourth mangles SILENTLY. The only reliable signal is the server's criteria_mismatch, never the shell's stderr.

THE CEILING IS A NON-RISK AND THE SCRIPT SHOULD SAY SO RATHER THAN GUARD IT HEAVILY. The circulated '8900-9002 bytes' figure is wrong. Re-derived: total URL 10016 OK / 10017 FAIL, bisected to one byte, 3/3 reproducible each side, a TOTAL-bytes limit not a per-parameter one. The mechanism is Bandit's max_request_line_length default of 10000 (5 + 9984 + 9 + 2 = 10000); over --http1.1 and direct to :4000 with Caddy bypassed the same byte returns a legible 414. Durable law: request target <= 9984 bytes. Per-criterion evidence budgets run 7197 (c6, tightest) to 9759 (c3); a proven c6 stamp spent 69 of 7197. Worker and epoch ride the BODY, not the URL. Have the script compute and print the remaining budget for the criterion being stamped so it is visible, and refuse locally if evidence would exceed it - an oversized stamp is fail-closed server-side (a 9000-byte sentinel wrote nothing) so recovery is 'retry shorter', never 'reconcile a half-write'.

corpus.title: An in-suite two-connection overlap test needs a harness outside the Ecto sandbox — today the outcome proof only exists in a hand-run

content.description:
SPUN OUT of task-bf3adebfec5833df when its criterion 3 was amended. Closing that row must not close this question.

That row REFUTED the concurrent-stamp lost update by run: 66 concurrent stamps accepted, 66 landed, 0 lost, with 120 of 120 writer pairs verified to overlap in wall-clock time. What shipped in PR #16241 is a SQL-shape oracle that pins the MECHANISM — the advisory lock is taken, it precedes the re-read, the update follows both, and the key is parameterised rather than a constant. What did NOT ship is a test that constructs the overlap, because the Ecto SQL sandbox cannot express a two-connection race in either ownership mode:

  {:shared, pid}  serialises every process onto ONE checked-out connection, so a "concurrent" second stamper QUEUES behind the first instead of racing it. A test written this way PASSES WITH THE ADVISORY LOCK DELETED — a vacuous green, which is worse than no test.
  :manual         gives each process its OWN transaction, so the task row inserted by setup is never visible to the second stamper. The race cannot even be set up.

So the outcome-level proof lives in a run somebody executed by hand, and nothing in CI would notice if the serialization were removed in a way the SQL-shape oracle does not happen to catch — a different mechanism with the same statements, say.

WHAT THIS ROW IS. A test harness that can run N real concurrent writers against real, separate database connections inside the suite, and the concurrency test for the stamp path written against it. It needs a deliberate opt-out of the sandbox for the tests that use it (checkout in :auto against a real database, with its own fixture creation and teardown), which is a decision about suite hygiene that deserves its own consideration rather than being smuggled in under a refutation.

NOT URGENT, and the row should say so. The invariant holds today and is pinned by an oracle plus a hand-run. This closes the gap between "we proved it once by hand" and "CI would notice if it broke".

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A test harness runs N genuinely concurrent writers against SEPARATE database connections inside the suite, and proves its own non-vacuity: with the serialization removed the overlap test REDS. A harness that cannot red when the lock is deleted has not solved the problem the sandbox created.

The sandbox opt-out is scoped and reversible: only the tests that need real concurrency leave the sandbox, they create and tear down their own fixtures, and a failure cannot leak rows into a sibling suite. Paste the isolation mechanism and a run showing the suite green twice in a row.

The stamp concurrency test is written against the harness and asserts the OUTCOME (all accepted writes land), not the emitted SQL. It supersedes nothing: the SQL-shape oracle in stamp_serialization_test.exs stays, because the two catch different regressions.

corpus.title: stage.ex documents its advisory lock key as doc_id while the code uses the UUID — a reader who trusts the docstring silently unlocks the stamp path

content.description:
FOUND while refuting task-bf3adebfec5833df, whose whole verdict turned on which key the close-family advisory lock uses.

stage.ex's moduledoc says its advisory lock is pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('task:' || doc_id)) — the doc_id SLUG. The code uses "task:" <> task_id and reads the row with Repo.get(Document, task_id), which is the UUID PRIMARY KEY. The code is correct and the invariant holds today: every close-family verb (close, release, move, stage, claim, pulse, stamp) keys on the UUID, so they genuinely exclude one another.

WHY A WRONG DOCSTRING ON A LOCK IS URGENT. Anyone re-deriving the invariant from that sentence gives stage a different key from stamp and close. Hashing a slug and hashing a UUID produce different lock ids, so the two verbs stop excluding each other and the read-modify-write on content.acceptance_criteria stops being serialized — which is exactly the lost-update hazard task-bf3adebfec5833df was filed about and which the code currently prevents.

AND NO TEST WOULD RED. The Ecto SQL sandbox cannot express a two-connection race in either ownership mode: shared ownership serialises every process onto one connection, manual ownership hides the fixture row from the second writer. The SQL-shape oracle in stamp_serialization_test.exs pins that stamp's key is parameterised, not that stage's key AGREES with it. So the regression would land green.

The fix is a docstring correction that names the UUID, states that the key is the invariant, and says what breaks if someone keys it on the slug — so the next reader cannot re-derive the wrong thing from it.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: stage.ex's moduledoc names the ACTUAL lock key — the document UUID via "task:" <> task_id — and no longer says doc_id. Quote the corrected lines and the code line they describe.

The correction states WHY the key is the invariant: keying stage on the slug while close and stamp key on the UUID hashes to a different lock and silently removes the exclusion between them. A bare value swap that leaves the next reader no reason not to change it back does not discharge this.
The correction records that no test would catch the regression, naming the sandbox limitation, so nobody assumes the suite is the backstop here.

corpus.title: Three honest misses are amended BY MEASUREMENT, and two paid rows are closed by content — no bar is moved and nothing is papered over

content.description:
LEDGER-ONLY SLICE. Touches NO code and NO gate files. Work through `bp`.

WHY. Wave 14 left two criteria that the evidence cannot satisfy, and wave 15's own review surfaced a third that is now STRUCTURALLY unsatisfiable. Leaving them is the "two honest misses sitting on the board forever" failure; deleting them papers over a real record. The precedent is the sibling epic's PDS wave 30 (PDS-D422, paid by PR #8648): an amendment is legitimate ONLY if it is PAID by measurement and RECORDS the measurement, not the opinion — and a rewrite that merely drops the demanding clause is BAR-MOVING and must be refused.

THE MECHANICS, AND THEY ARE NOT WHAT YOU EXPECT (charter D181). NO `bp task` VERB CAN WRITE A CRITERION'S TEXT. `bp task stamp` and `bp task close --set criteria:=[...]` share one merger in which the `criterion` key is read ONLY as a CAS guard — a mismatch aborts the whole write — and the writer touches exactly `met`, `evidence` and `attempts`. The sole path is a WHOLE-ARRAY document write:
  1. `bp task get <id> -o json` and copy the ENTIRE `acceptance_criteria` array.
  2. Edit the ONE `criterion` string in your local copy, preserving every other entry byte-for-byte including its `met` and `evidence`.
  3. `bp doc patch task <id> --set 'acceptance_criteria:=[...whole array...]'`.
  4. `bp doc publish task <id> --yes` — a patch writes a DRAFT and gates/boards read only the PUBLISHED ledger.
  5. RE-READ the published document and diff the array against what you sent. A printed rev is NOT persistence.
CONSEQUENCE YOU MUST RECORD ON EACH AMENDED ROW: the claim carries `work_field_digests.acceptance_criteria`, so amending the array will 409 the holder's later `bp task close` with `doc_changed_since_claim`; the close must carry `--set observed_rev=<current_rev>`. Put that sentence in each amended row's description so the closer sees it.

AMEND BY TEXT, NEVER BY INDEX — both index citations circulating in this wave's briefs are off by one. Match on the criterion's WORDING.

AMENDMENT 1 — `cch-w14-s3-fleet-row-band-899-split`, the "no `.fleet-row` height exceeds its 1440px-width height by more than 2x" criterion. THE MEASUREMENT: a 2x height bar cannot separate this fix from the shape GR65 already ships — the row's own reviewer recorded 2.25 as EQUAL TO the accepted 768 stack. Re-derive the ratio on origin/main for BOTH the shipped GR65 shape and the S3 shape, record both numbers, and amend the criterion to a bar that actually discriminates between them (or, if none does, to a criterion that names the two ratios and states that the height axis does not separate the shapes). Refuse any rewrite that simply deletes the clause.

AMENDMENT 2 — `cch-w14-s1-continuous-breakpoint-sweep`, the criterion demanding a full `--render` run whose worst `.content` top is 745.88. THE MEASUREMENT: 745.88 is dead on merged bytes. The value is 328 at H=800 and 282.77 at H=667, invariant across 320-720, both themes, and every cell — the pin went stale by MERGE ORDER (#8660 and #8655 are siblings that landed 45 seconds apart, neither an ancestor of the other), not by width. Amend the criterion to the measured values and the reason they moved, and record that `cch-w15-s1` deletes the pin outright rather than lowering it.
